plan.contextChunk: This figure is a plain vector diagram of four arrows stacked one above another, all drawn at the same shallow upward slope so their lengths can be compared at a glance. Each arrow starts from a small filled black dot. The topmost arrow, in dark navy, is by far the longest and is labeled 3v at its head. Below it an orange arrow labeled v runs in the same up-and-to-the-right direction at about a third that length. Beneath the orange one, a teal arrow labeled 1/2 v is half as long as v and again points the same way. The bottom arrow, drawn in red and labeled -v, has its dot at the right end and its arrowhead at the left, so it runs down and to the left while staying parallel to the others and matching v in length. Because all four share a single line of action, the only difference the eye registers is length, plus the reversal in the last one. The arrangement gives the geometric reading of multiplying a vector by a scalar: a positive factor stretches or shrinks the arrow while preserving its heading, and a negative factor turns it back on itself.

interactions.label: Scalar multiplier k
interactions.teaches: Positive scalar multiples keep the vector's heading while stretching or shrinking its length, k = 0 collapses the vector to a point, and negative scalar multiples reverse the direction

interactions.label: Layout
interactions.teaches: Stacking makes lengths easy to compare separately, while overlaying from one tail makes it clear that positive multiples lie on one ray and negative multiples lie on the opposite ray

demo_steps.title: Start with the original vector
demo_steps.narration: At k = 1, the scaled vector kv is exactly the original vector v: same length and same direction.

demo_steps.title: Stretch and shrink with positive scalars
demo_steps.narration: Move k to 3 or 1/2. The arrow stays parallel and points the same way; only its length changes in proportion to k.

demo_steps.title: Collapse at zero
demo_steps.narration: At k = 0, the vector has zero length, so the arrow collapses to its starting point.

demo_steps.title: Reverse with a negative scalar
demo_steps.narration: At k = -1, the arrow has the same length as v but points in the opposite direction, giving -v.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The sign of the scalar controls direction, and the absolute value of the scalar controls length.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean textbook-style SVG diagram with four parallel arrows at a shallow upward-right angle. In stacked mode, place arrows vertically one above another like the source: dark navy 3v on top, orange v below, teal 1/2 v below that, and red -v at the bottom pointing back down-left with its black tail dot on the right. In overlay mode, draw the same multiples from one shared black tail dot along the same line of action, with positive multiples extending up-right and negative multiples extending down-left. Keep labels close to arrowheads in italic math style.

- Slider for scalar multiplier k: the learner drags k from negative to positive values, the arrow length scales and flips direction when k crosses 0, and scalar multiplication is seen as stretching, shrinking, or reversing a vector.

discrepancies: A large extra purple dynamic vector labeled “kv” with a “k = 1” readout is present in the default view, but the source figure contains only the four static vectors 3v, v, 1/2v, and −v.

The generated figure places the vector tails well inside the canvas, whereas in the source the first three black tail dots sit at the left edge and the −v arrow extends off the lower-left edge, giving a tighter cropped composition.
The generated labels use “½v” as a single compact fraction glyph and bold colored/outlined styling, while the source shows a stacked 1/2 over v and simple black italic labels.
The static vectors are visually smaller and more spread out within a larger white plotting area than the source, which makes the composition less like the compact textbook figure.
The UI/control panel is visible beside the figure in the default screenshot, changing the appearance from a standalone static diagram.
evaluation.notes: The four intended scalar-multiple vectors are structurally correct and conceptually accurate, but the default rendering is not a clean drop-in replacement because it adds a prominent extra kv vector and uses a looser, less cropped composition.

Shift the static vector stack left so the first three black dots lie on or very near the left edge, and let the −v arrow extend partly off the lower-left edge as in the source.
Tighten the canvas framing and vertical spacing to better match the compact source composition.
Render the 1/2v label as a stacked fraction over v, or at least position and style it closer to the source label.
